data.title: Why Nvidia shares are down over 4% on Friday?
data.description:
Nvidia NVDA shares fell sharply on Friday as a broad selloff in technology stocks intensified concerns over the cost of artificial intelligence infrastructure and the time required for companies to generate returns on their investments.

Disappointing results from Amazon and Intel weighed on semiconductor stocks, while fresh reports involving CEO Jensen Huang and regulatory scrutiny of the company's acquisition plans added to the spotlight on the chipmaker.

Nvidia was down more than 4.8% trading around $203.40 at the time of writing.

The wider market was also under pressure, with the Nasdaq Composite falling nearly 2.5%, while the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average also traded lower.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped around 7% as losses spread across chipmakers.

Amazon and Intel results deepen AI concerns

Amazon's third-quarter results added to investor unease over the scale of spending required to build AI infrastructure.

The company reported a trailing 12-month free cash flow outflow of $42.4 billion, compared with a positive $14.8 billion in the year-earlier period. It was largely driven by increased investment in property and equipment, primarily for AI.

Amazon maintained its capital expenditure outlook of approximately $220 billion for 2026, reinforcing concerns over how quickly its investments will translate into stronger cash generation.

Its shares also came under pressure following the results.

Intel's weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter guidance further unsettled the chip sector.

Although the company beat third-quarter earnings estimates, it forecast revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion for the current quarter, below Wall Street's expectation of around $17 billion. Its adjusted earnings forecast of 25 cents per share also missed the consensus estimate of approximately 43 cents.

Intel shares plunged nearly 29%, while AMD dropped around 10%, adding to the pressure on Nvidia and other semiconductor companies.

Alphabet's results had already contributed to the technology selloff a day earlier.

The Google parent reported third-quarter free cash flow of negative $9.07 billion as capital expenditure on AI infrastructure climbed, while weaker-than-expected advertising revenue added to investor concerns.

Report raises questions over Jensen Huang's contact

Separately, a New York Times report published Thursday said US intelligence agencies had concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, an executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, was allegedly acting as a Chinese intelligence asset and passing commercial information to Beijing.

The report said surveillance had revealed that she developed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia rejected suggestions that the interactions were unusual, saying meetings with customers were part of the CEO's job.

The company also said regional cloud customers received ordinary business information, not sensitive trade secrets or information relevant to national security.

DOJ questions Nvidia's Hugging Face deal

Nvidia is also facing questions from the US Department of Justice over its proposed $12.93 billion acquisition of open-source AI platform Hugging Face.

Reuters reported that the department has asked whether the deal could give Nvidia control over an important distribution channel for AI and provide leverage over competitors.

The inquiry forms part of a broader examination of Nvidia's acquisitions, investments and sales practices.

The DOJ's questions do not establish wrongdoing or mean that legal action will necessarily follow.

data.title: Column: A hawkish Fed, shaky tech and the risk of an earnings letdown
data.description:
Markets are now heading into the last two months of the year, having closed out October with a flurry of significant events.

First off, the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, and Bank of Japan all held monetary policy meetings in the final week of October, and interest rates were left unchanged, as expected.

That removes a potential short-term headwind for equities.

Yet there’s still a general expectation that central banks will tighten monetary policy before the year-end, due to stubbornly high inflation.

Focusing on the US, the CME’s FedWatch Tool puts the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in early December at around 70%.

And if it once again chooses to leave rates on hold through to the year-end, then there’s less than a 10% chance that it won’t have hiked by mid-March 2027.

The interesting thing is that markets were more hawkish before the Fed meeting than after.

This is despite two FOMC members voting for an increase on Wednesday. Some observers considered that choice to be performative.

That could be the case, knowing that the majority wanted to hold, and given the problems that another hike would cause coming just a few days before the dreaded midterms – more in a minute.

But when it comes to pricing pressures, who can blame them? The major inflation updates released earlier this month were horrible.

September Core and Headline CPI both came in way above expectations and the prior month’s readings, with Headline being the highest number year-on-year since May.

Following this, the PPI data (the key measure of wholesale inflation, which typically leads consumer prices) proved to be even more shocking, with Core and Headline hitting highs last seen nearly four years ago.

To top it all, the day after the Fed left rates on hold, Core PCE, still the Fed’s preferred inflation measure and the one used for its 2% target, ticked up to 3.1% from 3.0%.

Not only is it moving in the wrong direction, but the last time it was below the Fed’s target rate was in February 2021.

Perhaps the Fed is hoping that a new virus will come and do its job for it again.

Failing that, if the tech sector selloff accelerates from here, the Fed could soon be cutting rather than hiking.

Bear in mind, the Fed, under its newish Chair Kevin Warsh, has made it clear that it will now be led by the data, rather than guiding the markets to a preordained route for monetary policy.

It has also said that getting inflation back down to its 2% target remains its number one priority.

Yet there was a dismal Non-Farm Payroll update in early October, along with an unwelcome uptick in the Unemployment Rate.

And it’s not the first time that payrolls have disappointed since the summer.

This has led some observers to wonder about the underlying health of the US economy once growth from the AI infrastructure buildout is subtracted.

That’s not to say that the AI trade isn’t genuine, only that it is highly concentrated and in danger of unravelling if certain optimistic assumptions don’t play out as currently priced.

And that brings us to the third quarter earnings season.

Earnings growth has been the biggest tailwind for US equity markets for years now.

And it is expected to continue into this quarter as well, with a year-on-year earnings growth rate forecast around 30%.

That could well come to pass. But results from Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon have really put the skids under the hyperscaler trade.

Meanwhile, and ahead of the upcoming Anthropic IPO, the only listed frontier lab, SpaceX, is trading at its lowest level in two months.

The chip sector looks like a bloodbath, and neoclouds aren’t looking particularly perky either.

Who knows how this will play out. Another ‘buy the dip’ opportunity?

Investors are now preparing for the midterm elections on the 3rd of November.

History shows that what happens after midterm elections has little overall effect on US stock market performance.

Corporate earnings, economic growth, employment, inflation and interest rates tend to matter far more.

Despite this, there have been times when politically sensitive sectors such as energy, healthcare and tech have faced different degrees of scrutiny following a change in control of Congress.

That can lead to a period of sector rotation, rather than the whole market moving one way.

Aside from this, a look at past midterms shows that political gridlock is a common outcome, and that often goes down well with financial markets.

The president’s party usually loses seats, and a split government is often seen as placing a limit on what an administration can do.

That could be considered a significant issue in the current political environment.

The polls close on the 3rd of November, and prediction markets suggest that a Republican-controlled Senate and a Democrat-controlled House are the most likely outcome.

This will be both an annoyance and a constraint for President Trump.

But it won’t affect his ability to issue executive orders, as well as deciding much of trade and foreign policy, including going to war.

So, as October draws to a close, the biggest challenge remains beating lofty earnings expectations. What could possibly go wrong?

(This is a fortnightly column by David Morrison. He is a Senior Market Analyst at Trade Nation. Views are his own.)

data.title: Why Intel, AMD and Broadcom are falling on Friday?
data.description:
Shares of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices AMD and Broadcom fell sharply on Friday as investors reassessed semiconductor demand following a dismal forecast from Intel.

The retreat was led by Intel after the chipmaker issued a weaker-than-expected forecast, while Amazon’s latest results added to concerns over the cost of building AI infrastructure.

At 11:30 AM EST, Intel shares plunged as much as 28%, putting the stock on track for its worst one-day decline on record. The selloff erased more than $120 billion from its market value.

AMD fell roughly 9.5%, while Broadcom declined around 5%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 6.65%.

Intel’s outlook disappoints investors

Intel’s third-quarter results beat expectations on adjusted earnings, but its forecast for the current quarter fell well short of Wall Street estimates.

Revenue rose 21% from a year earlier to $16.5 billion, matching forecasts. Adjusted earnings came in at 52 cents per share, above the consensus estimate of about 40 cents.

The outlook overshadowed that performance.

Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, compared with analysts’ estimate of around $17 billion. It forecast adjusted earnings of 25 cents per share, against expectations of roughly 43 cents.

The company also warned that gross margins would come under pressure.

A key weakness is the personal computer market, which remains a significant source of Intel’s revenue.

The company expects PC-related sales to fall by more than 20% sequentially in the current quarter.

Management pointed to a memory-chip shortage, as strong demand from AI data centres tightens supplies and raises component costs.

Higher costs and limited availability are weighing on consumer and business PC purchases. Intel expects the pressure to persist at least through the first half of 2027.

The forecast prompted analysts to lower expectations and renew questions about Intel’s competitive position.

BofA Securities downgraded the stock to Neutral from Buy and cut its price target to $100 from $145, saying Intel had yet to show enough progress in attracting outside foundry customers.

Roth Capital analyst Suji Desilva also moved to Neutral from Buy and reduced his price target to $70 from $120.

Morgan Stanley analysts led by Joseph Moore said the shares remained unattractive despite the steep decline, citing the risk that Intel could lose market share to fabless rivals with lower capital spending needs.

AMD and Broadcom caught in the selloff

AMD fell alongside Intel as investors considered the read-across for PC demand and competition in server processors.

AMD is due to report quarterly results on November 3.

BofA said weakness in the PC market could create a headwind of as much as $750 million for AMD, although stronger server CPU revenue could partly offset the impact.

Broadcom, a major supplier of networking equipment and custom AI chips, fell less sharply but was caught in the wider semiconductor retreat.

Despite its exposure to AI infrastructure demand, the stock moved lower alongside other chipmakers as investors reassessed valuations and spending expectations.

Recently, William Blair trimmed Broadcom from Outperform to Market Perform, highlighting increased valuation risks as the stock trades at over 40 times earnings. This puts shares at risk during sector-wide technology sell-offs.

Amazon adds to AI spending concerns

The pressure on the broader market intensified after Amazon reported its third-quarter results on Thursday.

The company recorded a substantial free-cash-flow drain linked to heavy investment in AI data centres, sending trailing 12-month free cash flow deeply negative. Amazon shares also fell.

The results revived questions about how quickly spending on data centres, chips and related infrastructure will generate returns.

Intel’s weaker outlook raised concerns about demand for traditional computing, while Amazon’s cash-flow figures highlighted the financial burden of AI expansion.

Together, the developments weighed on semiconductor stocks and broader technology sentiment.

data.title: Exxon earnings: $19B cash haul comes with a catch
data.description:
ExxonMobil’s (XOM) latest earnings give investors something more useful than another headline about soaring oil profits: a test of how much cash the business can generate – and how much shareholders should expect to keep receiving.

The energy giant reported third-quarter net income of $15.4 billion on October 30, with adjusted earnings of $4.23 per share beating the $4.08 LSEG consensus.

Refining strength helped drive the result, as disruptions to global fuel supplies boosted margins.

But the investment question extends beyond this quarter’s windfall: what survives when those conditions ease?

Refining reveals why Exxon is more than an oil-price bet

Exxon’s Energy Products segment earned $7.17 billion, edging past the $7.09 billion generated by its upstream business.

Compared with Q2, fuel-making profits increased while upstream earnings declined.

That divergence illustrates the value of owning businesses across the energy supply chain.

For investors, crude prices alone therefore offer an incomplete guide to Exxon’s prospects.

Refiners earn money from the spread between feedstock costs and finished-fuel prices; that spread can strengthen even when oil-production earnings weaken.

The implication cuts both ways, though.

Integration provides another source of earnings, but unusually favorable refining conditions can also flatter consolidated profitability.

Investors assessing future earnings should watch diesel margins alongside crude prices, rather than assume every business will keep contributing at today’s pace.

XOM’s cash cushion is substantial – but timing helped

Exxon generated $19.1 billion in free cash flow and distributed $9.4 billion through dividends and buybacks.

Its reported cash generation therefore covered those payments roughly twice over, leaving considerable financial flexibility.

However, working-capital movements contributed approximately $2.2 billion to operating cash flow.

Excluding those movements, operating cash flow fell to $23.4 billion from $25.7 billion in the preceding quarter, even as the headline measure increased.

That distinction matters because inventory, receivables and payment timing can shift cash between reporting periods without representing a lasting improvement in earning power.

Shareholders still received strong cash backing for their payouts.

But annualizing the headline free-cash-flow figure would risk treating a favorable quarterly movement as recurring income.

The more revealing test is cash generation across several quarters, after investment needs and working-capital swings.

The buyback promise sets up the next earnings test

Exxon also announced $20 billion of share repurchases for 2027, subject to reasonable market conditions.

The qualification deserves attention: it preserves management’s ability to respond if the operating environment deteriorates.

Buybacks can increase remaining shareholders’ ownership and support per-share earnings, but their investment value depends on the price paid and the cash available through the cycle.

A large authorization alone cannot establish that shares are cheap.

For prospective buyers, the strongest takeaway is Exxon’s capacity to convert favorable markets into financial flexibility.

The unresolved question is how much of that capacity persists under more ordinary conditions.

Friday’s results make cash coverage, refining profitability and capital allocation the measures to watch next.

Those will help distinguish a stronger underlying business from a particularly lucrative quarter.

data.title: Why are Micron, SK Hynix, and SanDisk stocks falling on Friday?
data.description:
Memory stocks including Micron Technology, SK Hynix and SanDisk fell sharply on Friday as disappointing earnings from Amazon and Intel triggered a broader sell-off in technology and semiconductor shares.

Micron MU declined about 5%, while SK Hynix fell over 7% and SanDisk dropped more than 10% despite reporting stronger-than-expected fiscal first-quarter earnings and issuing an upbeat outlook, as the stock got caught in the broader sell-off and analysts also flagged valuation concerns.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slid more than 6%, while the Nasdaq fell over 2%, reflecting growing investor concerns about the outlook for the technology sector.

The declines came as Amazon reported a third-quarter earnings and revenue miss, while Intel's weaker-than-expected guidance raised fresh questions about demand for chips and the cost of expanding manufacturing capacity.

Amazon and Intel results weigh on chipmakers

Amazon shares fell more than 2% after the company missed expectations on both revenue and earnings.

The e-commerce and cloud computing giant maintained its 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $220 billion, while reporting negative free cash flow for a second consecutive quarter, with the deficit widening substantially from the previous period.

Intel's outlook proved an even bigger drag on sentiment.

Its shares plunged around 29% on Friday after the chipmaker forecast December-quarter revenue below market expectations and warned that weakness in the PC market could persist through the first half of 2027.

The company also cautioned that it would burn cash this year as it contends with manufacturing bottlenecks, supply disruptions and heavy investment in production expansion.

The weakness comes despite growing demand for data-centre chips, as Intel has struggled to increase manufacturing output sufficiently to capitalise on that opportunity.

Higher memory prices are also pushing up PC costs, adding pressure to an already soft market.

"I'm disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter," Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on a conference call with analysts.

"We face near-term challenges, including manufacturing supply shortages, the unprecedented memory crunch, and the resulting softness in PC demand."

The warning reverberated across the semiconductor industry.

Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, Micron, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings' US-listed shares all fell.

China's CXMT reports surge in revenue and profits

The broader weakness in memory stocks coincided with strong financial results from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), highlighting the changing competitive landscape in the industry.

China's largest DRAM supplier by revenue reported a net profit attributable to shareholders of 54.4 billion yuan ($8.11 billion) for the three months ended September 30.

Its gross margin rose 1.94 percentage points from the second quarter to 89.53%, supported by higher prices and sales volumes and lower per-chip costs.

Revenue surged 613.2% year over year to 118.71 billion yuan, increasing 19.3% from the previous quarter.

The results marked the company's first financial report since its mammoth initial public offering in July.

CXMT has benefited from rising demand for memory chips driven by artificial intelligence, as established manufacturers such as SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics and Micron increasingly prioritise higher-value products, including high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

The Chinese manufacturer is now also seeking to expand into the lucrative HBM market, a direct threat to the three dominant memory chip makers- Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix.

Sources said this week that CXMT plans to begin limited production of HBM3E chips within two months, despite manufacturing yields of only 20% to 30%, compared with around 70% at South Korea's SK Hynix.

SanDisk beats estimates, but analysts flag valuation concerns

SanDisk's sharp share price decline came despite a strong quarterly performance and an upbeat outlook.

The company reported a 378% jump in fiscal first-quarter revenue to $11.03 billion, compared with $2.31 billion a year earlier, beating estimates of around $10.7 billion.

Adjusted earnings climbed to $49.51 per share, exceeding Wall Street expectations of approximately $46.67.

Its non-GAAP gross margin widened significantly to 85.1% from 29.9% a year earlier.

The company also issued stronger-than-expected guidance for the current quarter, forecasting revenue of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion and adjusted earnings of $55 to $57 per share.

It expects non-GAAP gross margins to remain between 84.5% and 85.5%.

SanDisk also repurchased approximately $5 billion of shares during the quarter and announced an eight-for-one stock split.

Shareholders will receive additional shares on November 19, with split-adjusted trading beginning on November 20.

The stock has surged more than 337% this year, making it one of the strongest performers in the memory sector.

However, analysts have begun to flag valuation risks following the rally, even as they remain positive on the company's fundamentals.

Goldman Sachs lowered its price target to $2,000 from $2,200 while maintaining a Buy rating.

The brokerage highlighted improving traction in SanDisk's data-centre business, including multiple enterprise SSD wins at hyperscale customers.

Data-centre sales now account for nearly 45% of revenue, according to the firm.

Goldman also pointed to the company's continued share buybacks and improving product mix, arguing that limited additions to NAND supply could support the market.

It expects shareholder returns through buybacks to increase further.

BofA Securities also cut its price target to $2,000 from $2,500, while retaining a Buy rating.

The firm lowered its valuation multiple to reflect concerns that the memory cycle could be approaching a late stage.

Wells Fargo expects SanDisk shares to digest a slowing pace of earnings upside despite another quarterly beat and higher guidance.

The brokerage said future share performance would depend on greater confidence in earnings stability across the memory cycle.

data.title: Evening digest: Binance hack rattles crypto, oil rises
data.description:
Cryptocurrency markets and technology stocks came under pressure on Friday as the $6.3 billion Binance hack renewed concerns about digital asset security, while oil prices climbed amid escalating tensions in the Middle East.

Gold and other precious metals also fell sharply as investors reassessed the outlook for technology stocks and interest rates.

Meanwhile, Intel shares plunged after the chipmaker issued a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the fourth quarter.

Binance hack: $6.3B crypto theft rattles markets

The $6.3 billion Binance hack has renewed concerns about cryptocurrency exchange security, triggering a broader sell-off in digital assets and crypto-related stocks.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said approximately $3 billion of the stolen funds had been frozen on-chain with the help of blockchain partners.

The exchange has pledged to cover customer losses through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds.

Teng attributed the breach to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allegedly allowed attackers to access a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

Binance said it had found no evidence of a private-key leak.

The incident also weighed on cryptocurrency-linked equities.

Coinbase shares fell more than 10%, reaching levels last seen in February 2024.

Circle Internet Group declined 9.5%, while Strategy lost 7.84%.

Bitcoin fell as much as 4.8% over 24 hours to approximately $76,820.

The attack has also raised questions about how stolen cryptocurrency can be recovered.

Stablecoin issuers, including Tether and Circle, have frozen funds associated with receiving addresses, while Bitcoin and Ethereum cannot be frozen through an equivalent issuer-controlled mechanism.

Binance has said customer balances remain safe and that it will cover the losses.

Investors will now watch the resumption of withdrawals and the exchange's updated proof-of-reserves report.

Oil prices: Brent settles above $117 as Iran war tensions intensify

Oil prices climbed more than 2% on Friday, settling at their highest levels since late April as traders assessed the risk of further escalation in the Iran war.

Brent crude futures for December delivery settled 2.32% higher at $117.55 a barrel.

The contract touched an intraday high of $118 before expiring on Friday.

The more actively traded January Brent contract gained 1.56% to $112.53.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 1.11%, to settle at $103.13.

For October, Brent gained 13.6%, while WTI advanced 15.2%.

Supply concerns intensified after a tanker was struck by explosive devices attached by a small boat in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency.

The incident highlighted risks to shipping through the strategic waterway, a major route for Gulf crude and fuel supplies.

Meanwhile, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed attacks on Saudi oil facilities, including the Ras Tanura and Rabigh refineries and a production facility in Abqaiq.

Gold price: Precious metals slide as technology stocks sell off

Gold prices fell to their lowest levels in a year on Friday, while silver, platinum and palladium also recorded substantial losses.

Spot gold dropped 3.44% to $3,881.68 an ounce, its lowest level since October 2025.

US gold futures for December delivery settled 3.46% lower at $3,891.10.

Silver fell 5.8% to $49.33 an ounce, breaking below the $50 level for the first time in 11 months. Platinum declined 3.68% to $1,438.50, while palladium lost 3% to $976.08.

The sell-off coincided with a sharp decline in technology stocks as concerns about the returns on artificial intelligence investments weighed on market sentiment.

Gold has now declined approximately 30% from its January record high of $5,595, amid expectations of higher interest rates for longer and weaker demand in Asia.

Intel shares plunge as weak Q4 forecast raises concerns

Intel shares plunged 28% in trading on Friday after the chipmaker issued a disappointing fourth-quarter revenue outlook.

The company expects December-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below analysts' expectations of $17.1 billion.

The forecast followed third-quarter adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, beating estimates of 40 cents.

Revenue reached $16.51 billion, slightly above the consensus estimate of $16.5 billion.

Intel also expects PC chip revenue to decline in the mid-20% range in the fourth quarter, following a 5% drop in the September quarter.

Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said the weakness in the PC market could persist into the first half of next year.

BofA Securities downgraded Intel to Neutral from Buy and cut its price target to $100 from $145.

Roth Capital also lowered its rating to Neutral and reduced its target to $70 from $120.

Analysts cited manufacturing constraints, weaker PC demand and competitive pressures as concerns.

However, Intel's expanding data-centre business and foundry ambitions remain potential longer-term growth drivers.

data.title: Anthropic IPO: Blackstone warns AI firm may receive junk credit rating: report
data.description:
Anthropic may struggle to secure an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its planned initial public offering, potentially increasing borrowing costs as the artificial intelligence company prepares for massive infrastructure spending.

Blackstone has told investors in Anthropic's latest $63 billion chip financing deal that the AI company is likely to receive a high-yield, or junk, credit rating following its IPO, said a Financial Times report citing people familiar with the matter.

The assessment marks a shift from Blackstone's earlier guidance that Anthropic could secure an investment-grade rating before the end of the year.

Blackstone is an anchor investor in the financing arrangement, known as Project North Star, and is working with banks involved in distributing the debt to other investors.

Anthropic filed to go public on Monday, potentially setting up one of the largest stock market listings next month.

Its prospectus outlined plans to spend more than $800 billion on computing infrastructure between now and 2045.

Anthropic's potential junk rating raises financing concerns

Blackstone has recently indicated that Anthropic is more likely to receive a rating in the double-B range or above, based on guidance from major credit rating agencies, the people cited in the report said.

A double-B rating falls below investment grade and could restrict the company's access to institutional capital.

Many insurance companies and pension funds face restrictions on taking large positions in borrowers with junk-rated debt.

This could reduce the pool of investors available to finance Anthropic's infrastructure expansion.

Consequently, the company may need to continue relying on suppliers with stronger credit ratings to support its borrowing arrangements.

An investment-grade rating is important to Anthropic's long-term financing strategy because it would allow the company to access debt at relatively lower interest rates.

Anthropic currently has more than $112 billion in cash and equivalents.

Investors also anticipate that the company could raise approximately $100 billion through its IPO.

A US technology-focused portfolio manager told the Financial Times that credit access was central to the company's financing ambitions.

Project North Star relies on Broadcom's credit backing

The financing concerns come as banks have completed the $63 billion Project North Star deal, which provides funding for Anthropic to lease 1.5 gigawatts of Google's semiconductors.

More than $42 billion of the senior loans is guaranteed by Broadcom, which co-develops the chips and holds an investment-grade credit rating.

The remaining $18 billion in junior debt is backed by Anthropic's lease payments.

Senior debt generally takes priority over junior loans in the event of a default, making it more attractive to institutional investors.

Broadcom's high A-tier credit rating was an important factor in helping Anthropic secure the financing.

Blackstone's funds invested $9 billion in the junior debt at a yield of more than 10%, according to the Financial Times.

Rating agencies assign different assessments to Anthropic debt

Project North Star's $18 billion junior debt has received a double-B-plus rating with a positive outlook from Kroll Bond Rating Agency (KBRA).

This represents a modest improvement from the stable outlook assigned to a similar financing arrangement, Project Big Sky, four months earlier.

Morningstar DBRS also assigned the junior debt a double-B rating, according to people familiar with the matter.

However, Fitch, Moody's and S&P, the three major credit rating agencies with significant influence over corporate borrowing costs, have not officially issued credit ratings for Anthropic.

Bankers representing Anthropic and rival OpenAI have reportedly lobbied major rating agencies to award the AI companies investment-grade ratings following their respective IPOs.

The uncertainty surrounding Anthropic's credit outlook also coincided with broader weakness in technology stocks.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 3.84% in afternoon trading on Friday following an earlier sell-off triggered by concerns about the sustainability of AI spending.

As Anthropic gets closer to its public market debut, investors need to watch out for the credit ratings the company receives, as they will determine its debt load in funding its AI buildout.

data.title: Rivian stock rises as analysts back R2 outlook after Q3 earnings beat
data.description:
Rivian Automotive shares RIVN rose on Friday after the electric vehicle maker reported better-than-expected third-quarter results and raised its full-year delivery guidance.

Analysts highlighted the R2 electric SUV, improving production prospects, and the company's autonomous driving technology as potential growth drivers.

Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) shares gained 4.76% at the time of writing, marking their biggest single-day advance in more than two months.

The earnings report prompted positive commentary from Wall Street analysts, with Jefferies upgrading the stock and Wedbush analyst Dan Ives maintaining an Outperform rating.

Jefferies upgrades Rivian stock as R2 targets market gap

Jefferies analyst Philippe Houchois upgraded Rivian to Buy from Hold while maintaining a $17 price target. The target implies approximately 45% upside from current levels.

Houchois expects Rivian's R2 electric SUV to benefit as US electric vehicle demand begins to stabilise.

The analyst pointed to what he described as a "relatively unique position and product void" in the 45,000-55,000 price segment.

He sees an opportunity for Rivian between Tesla's increasingly commoditised models and Ford's upcoming electric vehicle based on its Universal Electric Vehicle platform.

However, Ford's new platform may not experience a significant production ramp until late 2027, potentially giving Rivian an opportunity to establish its position in the segment.

Houchois also noted that Rivian shares had corrected roughly 30% over the past three months.

He considers the decline an attractive entry point as the company expands production and explores opportunities to license its autonomous driving technology.

Rivian shares reached approximately $20.20 in July before falling below $12.

Rivian raises 2026 delivery guidance after Q3 earnings beat

Rivian reported third-quarter revenue of $2.16 billion, representing 38% growth from the previous year. Its adjusted loss narrowed to $0.48 per share.

The company also improved its full-year adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) outlook to a loss of $1.75 billion to $1.85 billion.

This represents a $100 million improvement at the midpoint.

Meanwhile, Rivian lowered its capital expenditure guidance to between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion.

The automaker raised its 2026 delivery forecast to 67,000-70,000 vehicles, compared with its previous range of 65,000-70,000.

CEO RJ Scaringe said the R2, which began deliveries in June, had already become the company's best-selling vehicle, outperforming both its R1 models and electric delivery vans.

Rivian has also started a second production shift for the R2 at its Illinois factory.

More affordable versions of the SUV are expected to arrive through late 2026 and 2027.

Dan Ives highlights Rivian's autonomy and software potential

Wedbush analyst Dan Ives maintained an Outperform rating on Rivian with a $20 price target following the quarterly results.

Ives described the report as the "beat-and-raise quarter the R2 story needed", pointing to stronger-than-expected revenue, record deliveries and a narrower loss.

According to Ives, management expects the R2 to help drive the company's automotive business towards positive gross margins by the end of the year.

The revised delivery guidance implies fourth-quarter deliveries of between 25,000 and 28,000 vehicles, the analyst noted.

He also highlighted strong R2 demand and the introduction of a second production shift at Rivian's Normal, Illinois facility.

Beyond vehicle production, Ives pointed to Rivian's software and autonomous driving ambitions, including its joint ventures with Volkswagen and Uber Technologies.

The Uber partnership is expected to unlock another $250 million in equity by the end of the year, supporting a planned 2028 robotaxi launch.

Ives also identified Rivian's AI and self-driving technology as potential catalysts ahead of its December 9 Autonomy and AI Day.

He said these capabilities could represent an area of the business that investors have yet to fully value.

data.title: Binance reveals a $1B SpaceX stake: what happens if it sells its stake?
data.description:
SpaceX (SPCX) shares fell roughly 5% in trading Friday as tech stocks fell after Amazon and Intel's disappointing earnings.

Binance’s response to a massive cryptocurrency theft put its investment in Elon Musk’s company in the spotlight.

Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao said the exchange’s SpaceX holdings were worth more than $1 billion, raising questions about whether those shares could become a source of emergency funding.

Fellow co-founder Yi He subsequently said a sale of SpaceX stock was unnecessary.

For investors, the distinction matters: a potential seller has emerged in the conversation, but no disposal has been announced.

Why Binance’s SpaceX stake is suddenly in focus

The discussion followed a hack that drained $6.3 billion from Binance.

After Musk reacted to social-media commentary about the incident, Zhao pointed to Binance’s SpaceX investment while asking him to show support.

Yi He then said the exchange’s annual revenue was sufficient to cover the losses without selling those holdings.

That reassurance addresses the immediate liquidation concern, but it leaves an important financial distinction unresolved.

Revenue is not the same as profit or readily available cash.

Investors assessing the likelihood of a sale would need greater visibility into Binance’s accessible corporate funds, eventual recoveries, and reimbursement obligations.

Equally, customer assets under custody should not be confused with money belonging to the exchange. Their size alone cannot establish Binance’s capacity to absorb losses.

What would happen if Binance sold SPCX shares

A disposal would create additional supply of existing SpaceX shares.

It would not, by itself, dilute shareholders or remove cash from SpaceX’s balance sheet: proceeds would go to the selling investor.

The immediate market impact would depend on execution.

A rapid sale through the market could pressure prices, particularly during thinner trading.

A negotiated placement with institutional buyers could distribute the holding more efficiently, although buyers might demand a discount.

The psychological effect could extend beyond the actual transaction.

Traders anticipating a large seller may reduce exposure before any shares change hands, creating a temporary overhang.

However, neither the stake’s reported value nor Friday’s decline establishes how far SPCX would fall.

Binance has not announced a sale, and Zhao subsequently clarified that he had not proposed one.

A potential selling overhang is not an operating setback

For SpaceX investors, the central question is whether this remains a funding discussion at an outside shareholder or develops into an actual transaction.

A Binance sale motivated by reimbursement needs would reveal more about the seller’s liquidity requirements than SpaceX’s operating outlook.

It would not automatically signal weaker demand, deteriorating margins, or a change in the company’s competitive position.

Still, dismissing the issue entirely would overlook how markets price uncertainty.

Any subsequent announcement specifying sale size, timing, or restrictions could change the assessment.

For now, Yi He’s statement reduces the immediate forced-sale concern.

Friday’s decline is observable; attributing the entire move to Binance would go beyond the available evidence.

Investors should distinguish confirmed selling from speculation before treating this as either a lasting setback or an obvious buying opportunity.

data.title: Gold price crash accelerates as crude oil rises and odds of Fed rate hike jumps
data.description:
Gold price continued its downward trend, reaching its lowest level in months as demand waned after the hawkish Federal Reserve interest rate decision. It dropped to $3,925, down modestly from the August high of $4,700. This sell-off may continue as President Donald Trump prepares to escalate his attacks against Iran.

Gold price technical analysis

The daily chart shows that gold has come under pressure in the past few weeks, moving from a high of $4,700 in September to a low of $3,958. It has now crossed the important support level of $4,000 as it continued its series of lower lows and lower highs.

Gold formed a death cross pattern, which forms when the 50-day moving average crosses the 200-day moving average. This pattern often leads to more downside. At the same time, the Relative Strength Index (RSI) has dropped from the overbought level of 72.5

Therefore, these patterns suggest that gold may continue falling, potentially to the next key support level of $3,900. The risk, however, is that gold has formed a triple-bottom pattern whose neckline is at $4,700. This pattern means that sellers may attempt to push it higher in the near term. 

Gold price chart | Source: TradingView

Gold is falling as crude oil prices rise after FOMC decision

The ongoing gold price rally is happening as crude oil rally continues. Brent, the international benchmark, rose to $113, while the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) moved to $104. Higher oil prices mean that inflation will remain stubbornly high in the foreseeable future. 

Oil prices will likely continue rising after the US midterm elections in which Democrats are expected to win the House of Representatives and the Senate. President Donald Trump has warned that he will launch a short attack on Iran in a bid to put pressure on the IRGC to talk. Iran has warned that it will escalate if the US attacks it. 

The most recent data showed that the headline consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7% last month, while the core figure moved to 2.7%. Similarly, the headline and core personal consumption expenditure (PCE) remained above the 2% target during the month. 

These numbers mean that the Federal Reserve will likely maintain higher interest rates for longer. In its last decision this week, the bank decided to leave rates unchanged between 3.75% and 4%. Two officials - Beth Hammack and Lisa Cook - voted to hike interest rates.

In his statement after the Fed decision, Governor Kevin Warsh maintained that inflation remained stubbornly high and that the Fed will do whatever it takes to bring it down. As a result, analysts expect the bank to hike interest rates in its December meeting. 

Gold tends to underperform the market when the Fed is hiking interest rates and when bond yields are at an elevated level.
